source.title: Scaling Laws of Global Weather Models
source.authors: Yue-Jiang Yu; Lang-Wen Huang; A. Calotoiu; T. Hoefler

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. No apparent cutoff or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling behavior in global weather models, extending scaling-law investigations to a different domain and reporting its own results.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own data- and parameter-scaling results, fixed-compute allocation analyses, and comparisons of model shapes at similar parameter counts. Its cited language-model scaling results are not recorded as rows. Hyperparameter sweep outcomes used to select settings are not treated as scaling-law results.
record.test_reason: The study trains five global weather models on ERA5, a non-text domain. It fits its own power laws of validation loss against data and parameters, runs fixed-compute allocation sweeps and compares width against depth at matched size. These results bear on V5, and on V3 and V4 in a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also stress five further points: Aurora has the best data scaling (β≈0.51); GraphCast has the best parameter efficiency but poor hardware utilization; Pangu's parameter scaling depends on data volume; the constraint a+b=1 fails for graph models; and shallow models, even depth 1, work well.
record.recipe_differences: The study adapts scaling-law measurements to weather models: it varies ERA5 training-data volume, parameter count, and architecture shape, fits validation-loss relationships, and studies fixed-compute frontiers. Its metric is standardized weather validation loss, not language-model held-out cross-entropy; compute-optimal curves are analyzed with parabolas, and no small-run-to-large-run extrapolation is evaluated.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports model-specific scaling behavior, Pangu parameter-scaling changes between 15.0 TB and 30.0 TB, and differences in variable-specific scaling. It also reports that compute curves differ across model families and that hardware use varies substantially.

fits_no_version.finding: Variable-specific RMSE scales heterogeneously: Aurora is best on 10U, GraphCast best on 2T.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling gains and model rankings differ across forecast variables, so aggregate loss is a rough proxy.

fits_no_version.finding: Hardware utilization differs ~36× (Aurora 37.2% vs GraphCast 1.03% of H100 peak), so parameter efficiency does not equal compute efficiency.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: FLOP-based scaling laws omit wall-clock and utilization differences across architectures.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The compute-optimal analysis is limited by memory constraints and a maximum achievable width of 512. For Aurora and GraphCast, the reported compute curves mainly show their left halves because the models had not reached convergence; Pangu showed no clear loss-compute relationship. No uncertainty intervals or error bars are stated for the reported scaling fits. The paper says variable-weighted aggregate loss is only a rough indicator of performance.

untested.parts: Not tested: no language models or text cross-entropy.
Not tested: no extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
No fitted exponents a, b for N_opt or D_opt versus C, and no test of their stability across compute.
Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes are not tested; only deterministic 6-hour ERA5 forecasting.
No variation of fitting method or parameter counting. Exponent differences appear only across architectures and data volume.

missing.what: Per-model parameter-scaling exponents δ from the Figure 3 fits (e.g. 0.321, 0.188, 0.171, 0.136, 0.142), which are unassigned to models in the rows
Headline result: 10× more training data reduces Aurora's validation loss by up to 3.2×
CRPS scaling closely mirrors RMSE scaling. For GraphCast, CRPS degrades slightly once MSE converges.

record.verdict_notes: D is training progress within constant-LR runs, not independent dataset sizes. The text contradicts itself on Pangu: it says exponents are 'preserved' yet that Pangu's δ increases. The Figure 5 text and caption disagree about which models show clear minima. No uncertainty is reported on any fit. V4 was treated as limits_scope rather than challenges, because the version concerns language models and the study tests weather models.

versions.untested_parts: The study concerns weather models and validation loss, not language models' held-out pretraining cross-entropy.
It does not report whether fits from small runs predict the losses of runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study reports qualitative compute-optimal allocation findings but does not fit or report power-law exponents for optimal parameter count and training-data count as functions of compute.
Tests weather-model configurations at similar, not exactly identical, parameter counts; does not test language models or quantify the size of the shape effect over a wide range.
Tests deterministic global weather forecasting on ERA5. Does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study evaluates weather-forecasting loss and variable-specific errors, not downstream tasks predicted from language-model pretraining loss or scale.
It does not systematically vary fitting methods or other setup choices to test their effect on fitted laws; it does report model- and data-regime differences in its weather experiments.

rows.subject: Aurora

rows.note: The paper identifies Aurora as having the steepest data-scaling exponent among the five models.
rows.check: D is cumulative samples seen during single constant-LR runs, not separate runs. The D range is about 10–300 TB (~1.5 orders). Figure 2 gives two fits per model (0.508/0.497 for Aurora); Table 1 reports one β.

rows.subject: Aurora
rows.operation_detail: Compared a narrower, deeper configuration with a wider, shallower configuration at similar parameter counts.

rows.value: The wide configuration achieves superior performance; the paper says wider configurations consistently achieve lower validation loss.
rows.note: The paper describes width as more efficient than depth at closely matched parameter counts; the size of the loss difference is not stated.

relationships.reason: Each model fits L(D)=αD^-β (β≈0.34–0.51). The authors state that all five show power-law L(N) at both data sizes (r1–r6).

relationships.reason: At 15 TB, Pangu's δ is lower than other models' and rises at 30 TB, so its parameter scaling is data-bottlenecked (r7). The fitted ranges span only ~1.5 orders in D.
relationships.display_finding: Pangu's parameter-scaling exponent was lower than other models' at 15 TB and increased at 30 TB, with fitted data ranges spanning about 1.5 orders of magnitude.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Pangu's smaller exponent at 15 TB still describes power-law scaling. Its increase at 30 TB establishes data-dependent scaling efficiency, not a failure of V5's power-law form. Limited fitted ranges restrict extrapolation evidence without showing a departure from that form.

relationships.reason: The parabolas show a trade-off, but the text says Aurora's are only left halves (unconverged), and no stable power-law N_opt or D_opt is fitted (r8, r10).
relationships.display_finding: Loss curves showed an allocation trade-off, but the text described Aurora's curves as unconverged, and stable optimal parameter or data powers were not estimated.
